body.html:
Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks (280 days) from the last menstrual period, or 38 weeks (266 days) from fertilisation, which occurs about two weeks after the period starts. The organism is an embryo until the end of week 8 after fertilisation (week 10 of pregnancy) and a fetus afterwards; by the end of week 12 the fetus fills the uterus. The main outcome of the embryonic period is the formation of all organ systems; the fetal period is mainly growth and maturation.

Growth in length is fastest in months 3-5; weight gain in months 8-9. The head, half the length at month 3, is about a third at month 5 and a quarter at birth.

Weeks 9-12: low-set ears, fused eyelids, primary ossification centres, external genitalia alike until week 12, the physiological hernia returns, liver, pancreas and kidneys start working, swallowing begins; about 5 cm long.

Weeks 13-16: the placenta takes over, rapid growth, coordinated limb movements, breathing movements, slow eye movements, recognisable genitalia, ovaries with primordial follicles.

Weeks 17-20: quickening (movements felt by the mother, around the fifth month), lanugo and eyebrows, skin covered by vernix caseosa (protects the skin from the fluid), brown fat (oxidises lipids to make heat), descent of the testes begins.

Weeks 21-25: sucking, rapid eye movements, type II pneumocytes begin to make surfactant (lowers surface tension in the alveoli). Birth now is possible but with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disability.

Weeks 26-29: the age of viability: lungs and CNS mature enough to sustain breathing and temperature; the spleen's blood production passes to the bone marrow by about 28 weeks. Weeks 30-38: pupillary light reflex, pink smooth skin, fat on the limbs, testes fully descended; from 32 weeks babies usually survive well; at term length over 36 cm (crown-rump) and weight 2.5-3.5 kg.

Full term 37-40 weeks; preterm before 37 weeks; post-maturity beyond 42 weeks. Normal birth weight 2500-4000 g; low birth weight < 2500 g; small for gestational age below the 10th percentile. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) means failure to reach the genetically determined size, a slowed growth rate rather than a birth-weight cut-off. Causes: placental insufficiency, hypertension, multiple pregnancy, infections, cardiovascular anomalies, teratogens, genetic disorders.

Factors influencing fetal growth: maternal chronic illness (hypertension, diabetes, renal, cardiac, hormonal and autoimmune disease), smoking and alcohol, multiple pregnancy, impaired uteroplacental blood flow and genetic factors.

Ultrasound confirms the pregnancy and its site, then fetal size, twins, placental position and malformations (mid-trimester scan), and growth and position for delivery (last trimester). Amniocentesis for chromosomes and genetic disease; chorionic villus sampling at 10-12 weeks gives earlier karyotypes and is used for carrier-related conditions such as cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs and sickle cell disease; cordocentesis and spectrophotometry complete the list (see the fetal membranes lecture).

Ectoderm: surface ectoderm (epidermis, hair, nails, lens, enamel), neuroectoderm (neural tube: brain, spinal cord, retina) and the neural crest. The notochord comes from the primitive streak.

Mesoderm: muscles of the head, skeletal muscles, skeleton (ribs, vertebrae), dermis, connective tissue, the urogenital system (gonads, ducts, glands), visceral muscle and connective tissue, serous membranes (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum), the heart, blood and lymphatic cells, the spleen and the suprarenal cortex. Endoderm: epithelium of the gut and respiratory tract and the glands budding from them.

Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites, the first sign of segmentation. Their number is used to date the embryo: they appear in week 4 and reach about 42-44 pairs by the end of week 5. Somites give most of the axial skeleton, its musculature and the dermis of the skin. The intraembryonic coelom (body cavity) forms in the mesoderm lateral to them.

In week 4 the flat trilaminar disc becomes a cylinder, by folding in the median plane (head and tail folds) and the horizontal plane (lateral folds). Head fold: the primordial heart, pericardial coelom and oropharyngeal membrane move to the ventral surface; part of the umbilical vesicle is incorporated as the foregut; the septum transversum comes to lie caudal to the heart. Tail fold: the primitive streak, first cranial to the cloacal membrane, ends up caudal; part of the endoderm forms the hindgut; the connecting stalk and allantois move ventrally.

Lateral folds: form the abdominal walls and the midgut, which communicates with the umbilical vesicle through the omphaloenteric (vitelline) duct; the connection between intra- and extraembryonic coelom narrows; the amniotic cavity expands to surround the embryo.

Blood formation moves from site to site: yolk sac weeks 3-8, liver from week 6 until birth, spleen weeks 10-28, bone marrow from week 18 onwards. Until about age 5 all marrow is active; afterwards mainly the marrow of the flat bones and axial skeleton.

Week 4: head and tail folding, pharyngeal arches, heart pumping, closure of neuropores, limb buds, otic pits and lens placodes, tail-like caudal end, start of haematopoiesis, chorionic villi, mesonephric ridges. Week 5: rapid growth of brain and face, limb development. Week 6: reflex response to touch, auricular hillocks, physiological umbilical herniation. Week 7: digits on the hand plates, ossification of upper limb bones begins. Week 8: purposeful limb movements, scalp vascular plexus, neck, human appearance; the head is half the embryo.

A teratogen is any agent (viral, bacterial, chemical, environmental) that causes abnormal development; the embryonic period (organogenesis) is the most sensitive. Examples: alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome: cognitive deficits, heart damage, growth retardation, microcephaly), aspirin (deficits in attention and motor skills), caffeine (lower birth weight), cocaine and heroin (growth retardation, newborn irritability).

Embryology studies development from the fertilisation of a female gamete by a male gamete through the growth and differentiation that build a complex, independent organism. Ontogeny (life cycle) runs from fertilisation to death: the prenatal period (fertilisation to delivery) and the postnatal period (delivery to death).

The body has two cell types: somatic cells, diploid (46 chromosomes), made by mitosis for growth and repair; and germ cells, which by meiosis produce the haploid gametes (23 chromosomes), the only haploid cells of the body. Germ cells arise from primordial germ cells, first seen in the wall of the umbilical vesicle (yolk sac) and migrating to the gonads.

The somatic cell cycle: G1 (growth, biosynthesis), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), M (mitosis and cytokinesis); G0 is a resting state. Mitosis gives two identical diploid cells.

Meiosis has two divisions. Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes pair into tetrads, exchange segments by crossing-over at chiasmata, and separate (reductional division). Meiosis II: the centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate, like mitosis. Result: four haploid cells, each a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes. So meiosis differs from mitosis by haploid products, reciprocal exchange between non-sister chromatids and random assortment.

Starts at puberty in the seminiferous tubules (250-1000 per testis); sperm become motile and able to fertilise in the epididymis, where they are stored. Route: seminiferous tubules → straight tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis → ductus deferens → ejaculatory duct.

Cells, from basal lamina to lumen: spermatogonia (type A stem cells, type B committed) → primary spermatocytes (2n, 4N DNA, largest, prophase I about 22 days) → secondary spermatocytes (n, 2N, short-lived) → spermatids (n, 1N, 7-8 µm) → spermatozoa. Spermiogenesis is the final transformation, with no division: acrosome formation, condensation and elongation of the nucleus, flagellum, mitochondria arranged along the axoneme, and loss of cytoplasm as residual bodies phagocytosed by Sertoli cells.

Before birth, oogonia multiply by mitosis, then enter meiosis I and stop in prophase I as primary oocytes, each wrapped in flat granulosa cells: the primordial follicle. Their number falls to about 300,000 by puberty. After puberty, follicles mature: primary follicle (cuboidal granulosa, basement membrane, zona pellucida appears), secondary follicle (fluid-filled vesicles, theca, corona radiata), mature (Graafian) follicle with a single antrum, cumulus oophorus, theca interna and externa.

Just before ovulation, the primary oocyte completes meiosis I asymmetrically: a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body. The secondary oocyte starts meiosis II and stops at metaphase II; it completes it (with a second polar body) only if fertilised. The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, then the corpus albicans. Oogenesis gives one ovum per meiosis and has no metamorphosis stage; spermatogenesis gives four sperm.

title: Sperm transport, capacitation and the acrosome reaction
subject: subj:embryo1

body.html: Fertilisation usually takes place in the uterine tube (ampulla). Near the utero-tubal junction sperm attach to the epithelium (sperm reservoir). Freshly ejaculated sperm cannot fertilise: capacitation (5-7 hours, in the uterus and tubes) removes the seminal-plasma coat masking surface molecules and gives hyperactive motility. It allows the acrosome reaction: the outer acrosomal membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing enzymes to cross the zona pellucida. Fertilisation then proceeds in three stages: sperm preparation, sperm-egg binding and fusion, and the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy. The zygote gets its sex, its diploid number, and switches to cleavage by mitosis.

The antenatal period has three parts: germinal (fertilisation to implantation), embryonic (implantation to week 8) and fetal (week 9 to birth). Embryogenesis is how the embryo forms: fertilisation and implantation, bilaminar disc and uteroplacental circulation, gastrulation, neurulation, folding, somitogenesis and organogenesis.

Gastrulation (week 3) forms the three germ layers and starts morphogenesis. Its first sign is the primitive streak on the epiblast surface, with a primitive groove, a primitive node at its cranial end and a primitive pit. It fixes the cranio-caudal axis, the dorsal and ventral surfaces and the right and left sides. Epiblast cells invaginate through the streak: the first displace the hypoblast to form the endoderm, the next spread between the layers as mesoderm (mesenchyme: pluripotent embryonic connective tissue), and the epiblast left behind becomes the ectoderm. The prechordal plate (a signalling centre with Shh and PAX6 for the forebrain and eyes) and the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes remain bilaminar.

The streak normally regresses; a remnant can give a sacrococcygeal teratoma, the most common tumour of newborns, a benign germ-cell tumour of pluripotent cells removed surgically early.

Mesenchymal cells from the primitive node form the notochordal process, then the notochordal plate and finally the notochord, extending from the node to the oropharyngeal membrane. Functions: defines the axis, gives rigidity, is the primary inducer of the neural plate and the axial musculoskeleton, and contributes to the intervertebral discs (nucleus pulposus).

Neurulation: the ectoderm over the notochord thickens into the neural plate; its edges rise as neural folds around the neural groove, then fuse into the neural tube, the future brain and spinal cord. The neuropores close last (cranial around day 25, caudal around day 28). Neural crest cells leave the fold edges and migrate: connective tissue and bones of the face and skull, cranial, spinal and autonomic ganglia, heart septum, odontoblasts, dermis of face and neck, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, glia, meninges, melanocytes, smooth muscle of some vessels.

Neural tube defects: anencephaly (failure to close cranially) and spina bifida (failure to close anywhere from cervical to lumbar region), graded as spina bifida occulta (hair tuft), meningocele and myelomeningocele, which can paralyse the lower limbs. Abortion is termination before 20 weeks; almost all in the first 3 weeks are spontaneous, and about 50% are due to chromosomal abnormalities.

Folding incorporates the yolk sac into the embryo as the primitive gut, closed cranially by the oropharyngeal membrane (separating the ectoderm-lined stomodeum from the endoderm-lined pharynx) and caudally by the cloacal (proctodeal) membrane. Sequence: stomodeum → pharynx → foregut → midgut → hindgut → cloaca. The endoderm forms the epithelium and glands; the splanchnic mesoderm forms the muscle and connective tissue.

Foregut: primordial pharynx; thoracic part (lower respiratory system, oesophagus); abdominal part (oesophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, biliary apparatus, pancreas). The oesophagus reaches its final length by week 7 and is supplied by the vagus; its epithelium proliferates, occludes the lumen, then recanalises. Oesophageal atresia: 90% with a tracheo-oesophageal fistula; the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios); the newborn rejects feeds and an NG tube cannot be passed.

The stomach starts as a tube; its dorsal border grows faster (greater curvature) than the ventral (lesser curvature). It descends (from C2 in week 4 to T11 by week 12), tilts to an oblique position, rotates 90° clockwise around its long axis (left vagus to the front, right vagus to the back) and shifts left with the dorsal mesentery. The duodenum (week 4, from the caudal foregut and cranial midgut) forms a C-loop, is pulled right and becomes retroperitoneal; its lumen is obliterated in weeks 5-6 and recanalised by the end of the embryonic period.

In week 4 three buds grow from the duodenum: the hepatic diverticulum and the ventral and dorsal pancreatic buds. The hepatic diverticulum extends into the septum transversum: its large cranial part becomes the liver, its small caudal part the gallbladder; rapid growth from week 5 to 10. Endoderm gives hepatocytes and bile duct epithelium; the septum transversum mesoderm gives Kupffer cells, haematopoietic cells and connective tissue; sinusoids form around the umbilical and vitelline veins. Fetal liver: haematopoiesis from week 6 to birth, albumin from week 5, bile from week 12 (dark-green meconium from the 4th month), glycogen late. The ventral bud rotates behind the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud; insulin secretion starts around week 10.

The spleen is mesodermal, a mass of mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium from week 5; the stomach's rotation carries it to the left, linked by the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

In week 5 the midgut is a simple loop suspended by the dorsal mesentery and connected to the umbilical vesicle by the vitelline duct. Its cranial limb forms the distal duodenum, jejunum and proximal ileum; its caudal limb the distal ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. In week 6 the growing loop and the large liver leave no room, so the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord (physiological hernia); it returns by week 10, the caecum last. Taking the caecum as a landmark, the gut rotates 270° anticlockwise: 90° during herniation, 180° during the return, then the caecum descends to the right iliac fossa.

A persistent proximal vitelline duct is Meckel's diverticulum: the 'rule of 2s', about 2% of people, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocaecal junction, about 2 inches long, male to female 2:1.

Hindgut: left third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, upper anal canal, and the epithelium of the bladder and most of the urethra. The allantois appears on day 16; tail folding (day 26) forms the cloaca, into which both hindgut and allantois open; the urorectal septum divides it. The anal canal above the pectinate line comes from the hindgut, below it from the ectodermal anal pit.

Anomalies: omphalocele (about 1 in 5000; gut, even liver, in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus; 50% with other anomalies), umbilical hernia (covered by skin, mostly omentum, often closes as the linea alba strengthens), gastroschisis (defect in the abdominal wall beside the umbilicus, no covering), non-rotation (small bowel on the right, colon on the left) with risk of volvulus, situs inversus, intussusception, atresias of jejunum, ileum or colon, subhepatic caecum, Hirschsprung disease (congenital megacolon: absent parasympathetic ganglia from failed neural crest migration) and anal atresia / imperforate anus (about 1 in 5000, more in males, 90% with an external fistula).

Note: two slide slips corrected here: the stomach's rotation moves the vagus nerves (CN X, not CN XI), and Meckel's diverticulum lies about 2 feet, not 2 metres, from the ileocaecal junction.

Fertilisation has three stages: sperm preparation (capacitation, acrosome reaction), sperm-egg binding and fusion, and the cortical reaction. The sperm crosses the corona radiata, the zona pellucida and the oocyte membrane. As soon as it enters, the zona pellucida becomes impermeable (block to polyspermy), the oocyte completes meiosis II (female pronucleus plus second polar body) and the sperm head swells into the male pronucleus.

Results: restoration of the diploid number, determination of sex (X or Y sperm) and initiation of cleavage, in which divisions are mitotic without growth.

The zygote divides into blastomeres while travelling down the tube, becomes a solid morula, then a blastocyst, the first stage with a cavity. The zona pellucida prevents premature implantation, allowing safe passage through the uterine tube; it disappears before implantation. The blastocyst has two parts: the trophoblast (outer cell mass, future placenta and membranes) and the embryoblast (inner cell mass, future embryo).

Implantation begins at the end of week 1 (about day 6-7) and is completed in week 2. The trophoblast divides into the cytotrophoblast (the layer that forms new cells) and the syncytiotrophoblast (a multinucleated mass that invades the endometrium and secretes hormones). The endometrium contributes microvilli, adhesion molecules, cytokines, prostaglandins, enzymes, growth factors and extracellular matrix.

The syncytiotrophoblast secretes β-hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum producing oestrogen and progesterone and is the basis of the blood pregnancy test. The decidual reaction is the endometrium's response: its cells store nutrients and create an immunosuppressive environment for the implanting blastocyst. Progesterone, given for recurrent early miscarriage, acts on receptors in the endometrium.

Week 2 is the 'week of twos': (i) the trophoblast forms two layers; (ii) the embryoblast forms two layers, epiblast and hypoblast (the bilaminar embryonic disc); (iii) two cavities form, the amniotic cavity (future water bag) and the umbilical vesicle (yolk sac, primary then secondary); (iv) the uteroplacental circulation begins as syncytiotrophoblast lacunae open into maternal sinusoids and primary chorionic villi appear; (v) the extraembryonic mesoderm splits into somatic and splanchnic layers around the chorionic cavity. By the end of week 2 the connecting stalk is the only link between embryo and trophoblast; the prechordal plate marks the future cranial end.

Implantation outside the uterine cavity, most often in the uterine tube, is an ectopic pregnancy; a missed period with an abnormally low β-hCG raises that suspicion.

The fetal membranes are the amnion, the umbilical vesicle (yolk sac), the allantois and the chorion. Like the placenta they come from the blastocyst's outer cell mass and never form the embryo; they protect, nourish, excrete, support growth hormonally and act as an immune barrier.

The amniotic membrane = amniotic cells + extraembryonic mesoderm; it surrounds the amniotic cavity; together they form the amniotic sac, which secretes the fluid; amnion + chorion fuse as the amniochorionic membrane. Fluid comes from amniotic cells, diffusion across the amniochorionic membrane and, later, fetal urine; it circulates by fetal swallowing, absorption in the gut and airways, and return to the blood. Volume: about 30 mL at 10 weeks, 450 mL at 20 weeks, 800-1000 mL at 37 weeks.

Functions: mechanical cushion, prevents adhesion of the fetus, allows movement, maintains homeostasis (temperature), fetal lung development, prenatal diagnosis and dilation of the cervix in labour.

Polyhydramnios (> 2000 mL): often idiopathic, or the fetus cannot swallow (digestive or CNS anomalies, e.g. oesophageal atresia, anencephaly). Oligohydramnios (< 500 mL): placental insufficiency or urinary tract anomalies (renal agenesis); complications include pulmonary hypoplasia, limb defects and cord compression. Early membrane rupture can cause amniotic bands that constrict limbs.

Umbilical vesicle (yolk sac): transfers nutrients in weeks 2-3; gives the primordial germ cells in week 3; forms blood islands (weeks 3-6); in week 4 part of it is incorporated as the primitive gut, which gives the trachea, bronchi, lungs and alimentary canal. Allantois: an outpouching from the yolk sac wall into the connecting stalk; it becomes the urachus, then the median umbilical ligament. The umbilical cord contains the yolk sac and vitelline duct with its vessels, the connecting stalk with the allantois remnant, and the umbilical vessels in Wharton's jelly.

An embryo is the organism from fertilisation to the start of the third month; afterwards it is a fetus. Ultrasound (no known harm, cheap): fetal size, multiple pregnancy, placental site, abnormalities, guiding biopsies; mid-trimester scan for malformations, twins and placenta; last-trimester scan for size, growth and position. Fetal age is estimated from somite number, crown-rump length (first trimester), crown-heel length, weight, external features, biparietal diameter and head circumference (weeks 16-30), abdominal circumference, femur and foot length.

Amniocentesis (15-18 weeks): chromosomes, neural tube defects, genetic disorders; indications: advanced maternal age, risk of genetic disorder, parental chromosomal anomaly, previous spina bifida, inborn errors of metabolism. AFP is high in amniotic fluid (and maternal serum) with open neural tube and abdominal wall defects, and low in maternal serum in Down syndrome. Chorionic villus sampling (10-12 weeks): trophoblast biopsy for karyotype, slightly higher miscarriage risk. Cordocentesis (after 18 weeks): fetal blood. Spectrophotometry of amniotic fluid grades haemolytic disease. Fetal therapy: transfusion, fetoscopy, medication, surgery (e.g. a bladder catheter for urinary obstruction).

At delivery three things are born: the baby, the placenta and the fetal membranes. Membranes and placenta come from the outer cell mass (trophoblast) and never form part of the embryo. Their functions: protection, nutrition and excretion, endocrine support of fetal growth and an immunological barrier.

Trophoblast = cytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast; the chorionic sac = trophoblast + extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, enclosing the chorionic cavity. The trophoblast's proteolytic enzymes erode decidual vessels and glands; lacunae in the syncytiotrophoblast fuse into the intervillous spaces. Villi progress from primary to secondary to tertiary (with fetal capillaries); anchoring villi and the cytotrophoblastic shell hold the sac to the endometrium. Functions of the chorionic sac: metabolite exchange and hormone production (hCG).

Abnormal trophoblast growth: hydatidiform mole, with many fluid-filled cysts, usually benign but can invade and turn malignant as choriocarcinoma; the most common gestational trophoblastic tumour.

title: Parts and timeline of the placenta
subject: subj:embryo1

body.html:
The chorion becomes bushy at the embryonic pole, chorion frondosum, and smooth at the opposite pole, chorion laeve. The placenta has a fetal part (chorion frondosum) and a maternal part (decidua basalis).

Timeline: placental formation starts in week 3; vascular network in week 4; villi across the whole chorionic sac by week 8; placenta fully developed by week 12. At term, the villous cores become fibrous, calcium deposits obliterate some capillaries and the basement membrane thickens.

title: Placental circulation and the umbilical cord
subject: subj:embryo1

body.html:
Maternal side: uterine artery → 80-100 spiral arteries → intervillous space (~150 mL, renewed 3-4 times a minute) → endometrial veins → uterine veins → inferior vena cava → maternal heart. Fetal side: poorly oxygenated blood leaves the fetus in the two umbilical arteries → chorionic arteries → villous capillaries, where exchange occurs by diffusion → chorionic veins → the single umbilical vein, which brings oxygenated blood back. The two circulations never mix.

The umbilical cord links fetus and placenta. It contains the yolk sac remnant with the vitelline duct and vessels, the connecting stalk with the allantois remnant, and the umbilical vessels embedded in Wharton's jelly.

The placental membrane thins with time. Early (week 4): four layers, syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, extraembryonic mesoderm (villous connective tissue) and fetal capillary endothelium. By the fully functional stage the cytotrophoblast thins and becomes discontinuous, so exchange is easier. Gases, nutrients, wastes, some antibodies (IgG), drugs and some infections cross it.

The syncytiotrophoblast makes protein hormones, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), somatomammotropin (placental lactogen), thyrotropin and corticotropin, and steroid hormones, progesterone and oestrogens. Maternal IgG anti-D crossing the membrane destroys the red cells of an Rh-positive fetus: haemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis).

Dizygotic twins always have two amnions and two chorions (dichorionic diamniotic), with two placentas or one fused placenta. Monozygotic twins depend on when the embryo splits: early splitting gives dichorionic diamniotic twins (two placentas or fused); splitting at the blastocyst stage, the most common (~65%), gives monochorionic diamniotic twins sharing one placenta; late splitting gives the rare monochorionic monoamniotic twins. Shared chorions carry risks such as unequal blood sharing between twins.
